docs.title: Betaflight Setup for High-Rate IMU
docs.text: This document describes the configuration required to enable 2000Hz IMU streaming from Betaflight to NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX.

docs.title: Hardware Wiring
docs.text:
Jetson Pin (A603) Signal Name Betaflight Pad Note Pin 10 UART1_RX TXn Blackbox Data Stream (Requires RX/TX swap check) Pin 16 GPIO3_PBB.01 LED_STRIP HTE Sync Trigger Pin 6 GND GND Common Reference

[!CAUTION] If you receive 0 bytes on the serial port, verified by xxd or record_imu.py, swap the physical RX and TX wires. UART labeling is often inconsistent between boards.

docs.title: Jetson Configuration
docs.text:
1. Enable HTE: Ensure the Hardware Timestamping Engine is enabled in the device tree for microsecond alignment.

  2. UART Clock (80MHz): The standard 48MHz clock is insufficient for 1.5Mbps. You MUST set the BPMP clock to 80MHz: 

    echo 80000000 | sudo tee /sys/kernel/debug/bpmp/debug/clk/uarti/rate

    [!IMPORTANT] This setting is volatile. It MUST be reapplied after every Jetson reboot.

  3. Power Mode: Run the Jetson in MAXN mode for stable high-rate serial processing: 

    sudo nvpmodel -m 0
sudo jetson_clocks

docs.title: Betaflight CLI Configuration (4.5.x)
docs.text:
For Betaflight 4.5.x, use the following CLI commands to configure high-rate Blackbox streaming while manually stripping unnecessary parameters to reduce the UART payload size:

feature BLACKBOX
set blackbox_device = SERIAL
set blackbox_mode = ALWAYS

# Disable unwanted data to save bandwidth and simplify parsing
set blackbox_disable_pids = ON
set blackbox_disable_rc = ON
set blackbox_disable_setpoint = ON
# set blackbox_disable_bat = ON
set blackbox_disable_alt = ON
set blackbox_disable_rssi = ON
set blackbox_disable_debug = ON
set blackbox_disable_motors = ON
set blackbox_disable_gps = ON
# set blackbox_disable_rpm = ON
set blackbox_disable_attitude = ON  # Replaces 'mag' in newer versions

# Set the Blackbox rate (assuming 8kHz PID loop)
set blackbox_sample_rate = 1/1  # Target 2kHz on 8kHz loop (or 1/1 for max rate)
set blackbox_rate_num = 1
set blackbox_rate_denom = 4

# Configure UART1 (Serial 0) for 1.5Mbps for Blackbox
# Note: While MSP can be enabled, Betaflight prioritizes Blackbox when armed.
serial 0 128 1500000 57600 115200 1500000

save

docs.title: 🏗️ Deployment Architecture
docs.text:
The system utilizes a distributed ROS 2 graph to achieve low-latency perception and high-frequency control. The following diagram illustrates the data flow between hardware producers, processing nodes, and the flight controller.

graph TD
    subgraph "External Producers"
        Vicon[Vicon System] -- "Ethernet (UDP)" --> ViconNode
        Radio[Manual Radio/Joy] -- "USB/HID" --> Bridge
    end

    subgraph "Jetson Orin NX (ROS 2 Stack)"
        direction TB
        BB[blackbox_driver_node] -- "/imu0 (2kHz)" --> Ctrl
        ViconNode[vicon_client] -- "Pose/Odom" --> Ctrl

        Ctrl[drone_controller] -- "/drone_attitude_cmd" --> Bridge
        JoySub[/joy] -- "Override Toggle" --> Bridge

        Bridge[msp_bridge]
    end

    subgraph "Betaflight Flight Controller"
        FC[STM32 FC] -- "UART1 (1.5Mbps)" --> BB
        Bridge -- "USB-VCP (MSP)" --> FC
    end

    style Bridge fill:#f96,stroke:#333Msg,stroke-width:2px
    style FC fill:#bbf,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style Ctrl fill:#dfd,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px

docs.title: Data Flow Logic
docs.text:
1. Perception: High-rate IMU data is streamed via UART1 and processed by the C++ blackbox_driver_node. This node identifies 'I' and 'P' frames to reconstruct the state.
  2. State Estimation: The drone_controller fuses IMU telemetry with Vicon ground truth (or ArUco estimation) to compute optimal actuator commands.
  3. Control Injection: The msp_bridge node acts as a virtual RX. It consumes attitude rate commands and injects them into the FC via the MSP protocol over USB, bypassing the serial priority constraints of the primary UART.

docs.title: 🚀 System Launch & Configuration
docs.text: The primary entry point for the flight stack is the racing_bringup.launch.py. This launch file orchestrates the initialization of all hardware interfaces and control logic.

docs.title: Standard Execution
docs.text: ros2 launch drone_control racing_bringup.launch.py

docs.title: Launch Arguments & Options
docs.text: Argument Default Description shared_port /dev/ttyTHS1 Primary UART for high-rate Blackbox telemetry. rc_sim_port /dev/ttyACM0 USB-VCP port for the MSP Control Bridge. use_rc_sim true Enables the msp_bridge node for autonomous control. use_vicon true Enables the Vicon receiver for indoor ground truth. use_mavsdk false Enables MAVSDK (Requires MAVLink-to-MSP gateway).

docs.title: Overriding Parameters
docs.text:
You can override hardware ports or toggle features directly from the CLI: 

ros2 launch drone_control racing_bringup.launch.py rc_sim_port:=/dev/ttyUSB0 use_vicon:=false

docs.title: Manual Override (AUX2)
docs.text: The msp_bridge node respects a safety switch mapped to AUX2. * Manual Mode (AUX2 LOW): The msp_bridge passes through joystick/radio inputs to the flight controller. This is the recommended state for take-off and landing. * Autonomous Mode (AUX2 HIGH): The node ignores manual stick inputs and injects commands from the ROS /drone_attitude_cmd topic.

docs.title: Monitoring & Diagnostics
docs.text:
The msp_bridge provides a periodic heartbeat log at 1Hz to confirm active command injection: 

[INFO] [msp_bridge]: Sending MSP RC: R:1500 P:1500 T:1140 Y:1500 A1:2000 A2:2000 (OVERRIDE)
If the indicator shows (MANUAL), the drone will not respond to autonomous commands even if the node is running.

docs.title: 🛡️ Troubleshooting Refined
docs.text: If the msp_bridge fails to connect: 1. Check the USB connection to the Betaflight FC. It must appear as /dev/ttyACM0. 2. Ensure the user is in the dialout group: sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER. 3. Verify the port isn't locked by another process (e.g., Betaflight Configurator).

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Page Owner: Leads of the Aeronautics Division

This repository provides a ready-to-use drone racing environment using Docker. By containerizing the development environment, we ensure consistency across different host systems and simplify the setup of complex robotics software.

docs.title: Environment Overview
docs.text:
The environment bundles the following core components:

  • ROS 2 Humble: Our primary robotics framework.
  • Gazebo (gz): A high-fidelity 3D simulator for drones.
  • PX4 SITL: The autopilot software running in simulation.
  • MAVROS / MAVSDK: Communication bridges between PX4 and ROS.
  • Workspace (/ws): The location for custom ROS 2 packages.

[!IMPORTANT] Host OS: Ubuntu/Linux is highly recommended for GUI compatibility. Requirements: Docker Engine + Compose v2.

docs.title: Docker Infrastructure
docs.text:
graph TD
    B["<b>Base</b><br/>(Core ROS & Tools)"]:::m-base --> SPCD["<b>shared-perception-<br/>controls-deps</b>"]:::m-dep
    B --> D["<b>docs</b>"]:::m-dep
    SPCD --> P["<b>perception</b>"]:::m-target
    SPCD --> SMRD["<b>shared-mpc-rl-deps</b>"]:::m-dep
    SMRD --> M["<b>mpc</b>"]:::m-target
    SMRD --> R["<b>rl</b>"]:::m-target
    P --> DEV["<b>dev</b><br/>(Full Environment)"]:::m-final
    M --> DEV
    R --> DEV
    D -.-> DEV

docs.title: Build Targets
docs.text:
• base: The core foundation containing ROS 2, system tools, and base dependencies.
  • docs: A lightweight environment for building and serving this documentation.
  • perception: Specialized for camera-based tracking and state estimation (OpenVINS, Gate Detection).
  • mpc: Optimized for high-performance controls and trajectory tracking (MAVSDK, ACADOS).
  • rl: Includes neural network and reinforcement learning libraries (PyTorch, Stable Baselines 3).
  • dev: The complete, integrated environment containing all components above.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Follow these steps to get the environment running.

docs.title: Step 0: SSH Setup
docs.text: We use SSH for Git operations to avoid repeated password prompts. Follow GitHub's SSH guide here.

docs.title: Step 1: Clone the Repository
docs.text:
Ensure you clone with submodules to include the PX4 Autopilot. 

git clone --recurse-submodules git@github.com:ETHRoboticsClub/ETHRC-Drone-Racing.git
cd ETHRC-Drone-Racing
git submodule update --init --recursive

docs.title: Step 2: Build and Prepare
docs.text:
Build the Docker image and prepare the host volumes for ROS 2. We use multi-stage builds to provide specialized environments for different teams.

# To build the FULL development environment (Default)
docker compose build dev

# To build only for the Perception team
docker compose build perception

# To build only for the MPC / Control team
docker compose build mpc

# To build only for the RL team
docker compose build rl

# To build ONLY the documentation
docker compose build docs

Ensure host volumes are prepared: 

./scripts/prepare_colcon_volumes.sh

docs.title: Step 3: Start Services
docs.text:
Allow GUI applications and start your preferred container target.

xhost +local:root

# Start the full environment
docker compose up dev -d

# OR start a specific team environment
docker compose up mpc -d

docs.title: Step 4: Access and Build
docs.text:
Attach to the running container and build the workspace.

docker compose exec dev bash

# Inside the container:
colcon build --symlink-install --cmake-args -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo

docs.title: Build Command Breakdown
docs.text:
• --symlink-install: Instead of copying files, ROS 2 creates symbolic links to your source files. This means changes to Python scripts or configuration files take effect instantly without needing another build.
  • -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo: Compiles with optimizations (for performance) while keeping debug symbols (for troubleshooting).

[!IMPORTANT]

docs.title: 💡 Sourcing the Workspace
docs.text:
After building, or whenever you open a new terminal tab, you MUST source the workspace to make the packages visible to ROS 2: 

source install/setup.bash
If you omit this, you will see Package 'drone_control' not found errors.

docs.title: Flying the Drone
docs.text: Once the simulation and controller are running, you can command the drone using our standard goal-sending utilities.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Controller
docs.text:
In a container terminal, start the MPC controller: 

ros2 launch drone_control drone_controller.launch.py

docs.title: Step 2: Send a Pose Goal (Takeoff)
docs.text:
In a separate container terminal, use the send_pose_goal script to command a takeoff to 2 meters: 

ros2 run drone_control send_pose_goal goal_only -x 0.0 -y 0.0 -z 2.0 -yaw 90

docs.title: Argument Breakdown
docs.text: Argument Description goal_only Sends the goal and waits for completion. Use cancel to stop an active mission. -x, -y, -z Target coordinates in meters. -yaw Target orientation in degrees.

docs.title: Step 3: Monitor in PlotJuggler
docs.text: The controller launch automatically opens PlotJuggler. Look for the /drone_state_sim and /drone_current_target topics to verify the drone is tracking the reference accurately.

docs.title: Running Simulation
docs.text:
To launch the default simulation environment:

  1. Source the workspace: 
    source install/setup.bash
  2. Launch PX4 SITL with Gazebo (pick one): 
    cd /home/drone_dev/ros_ws/px4/PX4-Autopilot
make px4_sitl gz_drone       # ETHRC custom drone (airframe 4023)
make px4_sitl gz_x500_cam    # x500 with front camera (airframe 4022)

docs.title: Visualization and Monitoring
docs.text: Visualizing the internal state of the drone is crucial for debugging perception and control algorithms.

docs.title: RViz Visualization
docs.text: We use RViz2 to visualize sensor data, gate detections, and EKF state.

docs.title: Full Perception Launch
docs.text:
You can launch the integrated perception stack (VIO + Gate Detection + EKF) using: 

source install/setup.bash
ros2 launch launch/perception.launch.py

docs.title: Permission Errors
docs.text:
If you see permission denied errors during build or when accessing volumes, run the preparation script on the host: 

sudo ./scripts/prepare_colcon_volumes.sh

docs.title: Submodule Issues
docs.text:
If the build fails due to missing source files in src/perception/VIO or src/ros2-vicon-receiver, ensure your submodules are up to date: 

git submodule update --init --recursive

docs.title: Package Not Found After Docker Compose Up
docs.text:
If ros2 launch fails with "Package not found", the host's empty .colcon/install volume is masking the container's build. Rebuild inside the container: 

colcon build --symlink-install --cmake-args -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo
source install/setup.bash

docs.title: Native Execution (Non-Docker)
docs.text: While Docker is great for simulation and development on a workstation, you may want to run part of the stack natively on your companion computer (e.g., Jetson Orin NX) to reduce overhead or access specific hardware pins.

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Ensure you have ROS 2 installed on your host system (this project targets Humble, though it is compatible with Jazzy). 

# Example for installing colcon
sudo apt update && sudo apt install python3-colcon-common-extensions

docs.title: 2. Build the Workspace
docs.text:
From the project root: 

colcon build --symlink-install --cmake-args -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release

docs.title: 3. Fast Bringup (The "Big Button")
docs.text:
Once built, you can launch the entire racing stack across all modules (Comms, Perception, and Control) using the unified bringup script:

source install/setup.bash
ros2 launch drone_control racing_bringup.launch.py msp_port:=/dev/ttyTHS1

docs.title: 4. Configuration Tips
docs.text:
• Serial Ports: If you are using a USB-to-Serial adapter instead of the internal UART, use msp_port:=/dev/ttyUSB0.
  • Persisting Settings: You can edit the default parameters in src/betaflight_msp_controller/config/msp_params.yaml so you don't have to pass them every time.

docs.title: Project Guidelines
docs.text:
Page Owner: Leads of the Aeronautics Division

This document outlines the guidelines for contributing to the ETHRC Drone Racing project, including documentation standards and development workflow.

docs.title: Documentation Guidelines
docs.text: We use MkDocs with the Material for MkDocs theme.

docs.title: Editing Documentation
docs.text:
Documentation source files are located in docs/docs/. They are written in Markdown, this is a really useful guide by Google.

  • Headers: Use # for page titles and ## for section headers.
  • Code Blocks: Use triple backticks (```) for code blocks. Specify the language for syntax highlighting (e.g., ```bash).
  • Images: Place images in docs/docs/images/ and reference them as ![Alt Text](images/filename.png).
  • Admonitions: Use admonitions for notes, warnings, and tips: 
    !!! note
    This is a note.

docs.title: Running Locally
docs.text:
To preview your changes locally, run the following command from the docs/ directory (or root if using the Docker container):

mkdocs serve

The site will be available at http://localhost:8000.

docs.title: Git Workflow
docs.text:
We follow a standard feature-branch workflow:

  1. Create a Branch: Create a new branch for your feature or fix. 
    git checkout -b feature/my-new-feature
  2. Commit Changes: Make your changes and commit them with clear, descriptive messages. 
    git commit -m "Add new flight controller logic"
  3. Push and PR: Push your branch to GitHub and open a Pull Request (PR) against main.
  4. Review and Merge: After review, merge the PR. Delete the branch after merging.

docs.title: Agent Development (AI Assistants)
docs.text:
If you are an AI assistant (e.g., Antigravity, Claude, Codex) helping with development:

  • Read the guidelines: First, read the guidelines in this document and the detailed guides in /aeronautics-utility/agents (as specified in the README.md).
  • Understand the code: Do not perform blind edits. Ensure you understand the surrounding code logic. If you are unsure, explain your reasoning or ask the user for clarification.
  • Manageable Commits: Break up the development into smaller, focused commits. Avoid overwhelmingly large commits (e.g., thousands of lines) that are difficult to review.

docs.title: Docker Environment
docs.text:
The project relies heavily on Docker to ensure a consistent environment.

  • Rebuilding: If you modify docker/Dockerfile or requirements.txt (if applicable), rebuild the image: 
    docker compose build
  • Running: Start the environment with: 
    docker compose up -d

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Page Owner: Controls Team

Welcome to the Controls team documentation. This section describes the control algorithms, flight stack configuration, and how components interact during flight.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The architecture is designed to be modular, controller-agnostic, and tightly integrated with ROS 2, while relying on MAVSDK for low-level communication with the vehicle.

docs.title: Codebase Architecture
docs.text:
At a high level, the control stack is organized around three main layers:

  1. ROS 2 control interface (drone_control)
  2. Controller implementations (MPC, RL)
  3. Low-level vehicle interface (MAVSDK / PX4)

Each layer has a clearly defined responsibility, allowing controllers to be swapped or extended with minimal changes to the rest of the system.

docs.title: drone_control: ROS 2 Control Interface
docs.text:
The drone_control module is the central ROS 2 interface for flight control.

It acts as the glue between: - The ground station - The perception and state estimation stack - The controller (MPC or RL) - The low-level vehicle interface (MAVSDK)

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
drone_control is responsible for:

  • Subscribing to ROS 2 topics providing:
  • State estimation (pose, velocity, attitude, etc.)
  • Setpoints and mission-level commands
  • System and control-related signals from the ground station
  • Managing the control logic and execution flow
  • Selecting and running the active controller
  • Publishing low-level control commands to ROS 2 topics

These command topics are then consumed by the MAVSDK client, which forwards them to the drone.

docs.title: Command Path: ROS 2 → MAVSDK → Drone
docs.text:
The control flow is as follows:

  1. State estimation and setpoints are produced by the perception stack and/or ground station and published on ROS 2 topics.
  2. drone_control:
  3. Collects the current state
  4. Passes it to the active controller
  5. Receives actuator-level or rate-level commands
  6. drone_control publishes these commands on a dedicated ROS 2 topic.
  7. MAVSDK subscribes to this topic and:
  8. Converts the commands to MAVSDK offboard messages
  9. Sends them to the drone via MAVLink

This design ensures a clean separation between control logic and vehicle communication.

docs.title: Controller Implementations: MPC and RL
docs.text:
The actual control laws are implemented in separate modules:

  • MPC: Model Predictive Control–based controller
  • RL: Reinforcement Learning–based controller

Each controller: - Consumes the current estimated state - Outputs control commands (e.g. body rates + thrust or per-motor thrust)

Currently, the MPC outputs body rates + collective thrust, (we just realize that MAVSDK can send per-motor thrust), it is planned to change the model to output per-motor thrust.

docs.title: Modularity Goal
docs.text:
A key design goal is to make drone_control fully controller-agnostic.

Any controller that follows the expected interface can be plugged in, without modifying: - MAVSDK integration - ROS 2 communication - Ground station or perception interfaces

At the moment: - The system has been validated and used primarily with MPC - The RL pipeline still requires: - Policy extraction - Runtime inference integration - ROS 2–level interfacing

docs.title: Current Status and Future Work
docs.text:
• MPC is fully integrated and operational
  • RL support is under development
  • Policy loading and inference need to be finalized
  • Interface alignment with drone_control is still required

The existing architecture already supports this extension, and only the controller-specific logic needs to be added.

For detailed information on each controller and their interfaces, please refer to: - MPC - RL - DRONE_CONTROL - MAVSDK

Troubleshooting: For troubleshooting of common problems, check General Control Troubleshooting

docs.title: Drone Control
docs.text: Page Owner: Michalis Papadakis

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This node implements the drone controller that receives the estimated system state and executes pose or trajectory goals via ROS 2 actions.

[!NOTE] The node is intended to be controller agnostic, allowing: 1. Multiple controllers to utilize the same interfaces. 2. Specialized controllers to handle different goals (e.g., LQR for hovering, MPC/RL for trajectory tracking).

To achieve this, the node uses two state flags: active_goal (indicates an active action) and hovering_active (indicates stable hovering state).

Note: Currently the controller only supports MPC for hovering, pose and trajectory goals, and needs modifications to support other controllers. The action interface is intented for task-specific controllers, the code needs to be improved for that.

All the parameters are configured in drone_controller_config.yaml

docs.title: Action Interfaces
docs.text: The node exposes the following ROS 2 action servers for goal-based control.

docs.title: Set Pose Goal Action
docs.text:
• Action Name: /drone_set_pose_goal
  • Type: FollowWaypoints
  • Description: Commands the drone to move to a single target pose
  • Behavior:
  • Accepts a pose goal only if currently no other goal is active
  • Disables hovering controller so pose controller can be activated
  • Executes closed-loop control until the target is reached with a specified threshold (specified by the threshold parameter) or the goal is canceled.
  • Finishing the execution, it launches a hovering thread that stabilizes the current state.

docs.title: Set Trajectory Goal Action
docs.text:
• Action Name: /drone_set_trajectory_goal
  • Type: FollowWaypoints
  • Description: Commands the drone to follow a sequence of waypoints (trajectory)
  • Behavior:
  • Accepts a list of waypoints only if currently no other goal is active
  • Disables hovering controller so pose controller can be activated
  • Executes closed-loop control until the target is reached with a specified threshold (specified by the threshold parameter) or the goal is canceled.
  • Finishing the execution, it launches a hovering thread that stabilizes the current state.

The helper nodes: send_pose_goal and send_trajectory_goal showcase the use of the action inteface and its pre-emption capabilities from the CLI and can be used for developement. Their used is shown below However, the GUI is the intented action client.

docs.title: Input Topics
docs.text: This controller node subscribes to the following ROS 2 topics:

docs.title: Drone State
docs.text:
• Topic: specified by state_topic parameter. (Default: drone_state_sim)
    • \drone_state_sim: For getting the state from mavsdk
    • <perception_topic>: For getting the state from perception pipeline
  • Type: std_msgs/msg/Float64MultiArray
  • Description: Current drone state vector (e.g., position, velocity, quaternion, angular velocity)
  • Frequency: sim: 200Hz
  • Queue Size: 10

These command topics are consumed by the MAVSDK client, which forwards them to the drone.

docs.title: Command Path: ROS 2 → MAVSDK → Drone
docs.text: The controller node publishes the following ROS 2 topics:

docs.title: AttitudeRate Command
docs.text:
• Topic: specified by attitude_command_topic parameter. (Default: /drone_attitude_cmd)
  • Type: std_msgs/msg/Float64MultiArray
  • Description: Attitude rate command sent to the drone (e.g., roll-rate, pitch-rate, yaw-rate, normalized-thrust). See AttitudeRate
  • Frequency: specified by controller_rate parameter (Default: 100hz)
  • Queue Size: 10

docs.title: Position Command
docs.text:
• Topic: specified by position_command_topic parameter. (Default: drone_position_cmd)
  • Type: std_msgs/msg/Float64MultiArray
  • Description: Position command sent in the earth NED frame. See PositionNedYaw
  • Frequency: specified by controller_rate parameter (Default: 100hz)
  • Queue Size: 10

docs.title: Current Target Pose
docs.text: This is used to visualize the active pose target in rviz and telemetry - Topic: /drone_current_target - Type: geometry_msgs/msg/PoseStamped - Description: Current target pose that the controller is tracking (e.g., active waypoint) - QoS: - Durability: TRANSIENT_LOCAL - Depth: 1 - Frequency: Updated on target changes or during trajectory execution

docs.title: Run the node
docs.text:
1. Run the simulation first: 

    cd ~/ros_ws/px4/PX4-Autopilot && make px4_sitl gz_x500

  2. Run the mpc controller, mavsdk client && plotjuggler visualization 

    ros2 launch drone_control drone_controller.launch.py

  3. You can test the controller from CLI with (this is a placeholder node, since this functionalities will be implemented using GUI):

    Important: Make sure drone is armed. At startup, if one does not give a command, it disarms automatically. One can arm it by: 

    ros2 service call /arm_drone std_srvs/srv/SetBool "{data: true}"

    Position goals: 

    ros2 run drone_control send_pose_goal goal_only -x 0.0 -y 0.0 -z -1.0 -yaw 0.0

    Trajectory goals: 1. Modify the yaml_file 2. Run 

    ros2 run drone_control send_trajectory_goal goal_only

docs.title: MAVSDK
docs.text: Page Owner: Controls Team

docs.title: What is MAVSDK?
docs.text:
MAVSDK (Micro Air Vehicle Software Development Kit) is a high-level, language-agnostic API designed to control and interact with MAVLink-compatible vehicles such as drones and ground robots. It provides an abstraction layer on top of MAVLink, allowing developers to communicate with an autopilot without dealing directly with low-level message handling.

MAVSDK supports multiple programming languages (C++, Python, Swift, Java) and exposes a plugin-based API for telemetry, offboard control, mission handling, parameter access, and system health monitoring.

In practice, MAVSDK is the bridge between PX4 and our code, running on the companion computer.

docs.title: PX4 Autopilot
docs.text:
PX4 is an open-source autopilot system running on the flight controller hardware. It is responsible for estimation, control, safety logic, and actuator outputs, and exposes its interface via MAVLink.

In our stack, we do not rely on PX4’s EKF nor on its internal cascaded PID controllers for nominal operation. State estimation and control are handled externally by our own pipelines (e.g. MPC, RL). However, PX4 remains available as a fallback: its estimator and controllers can be re-enabled if needed for safety, debugging, or recovery.

We chose PX4 because it is:

  • Highly modular and well-structured
  • Supported by a rich ecosystem of tools:
  • Software-In-The-Loop (SITL) with Gazebo
  • Hardware-In-The-Loop (HITL)
  • Backed by a large and active community
  • Fully compatible with MAVSDK

While our long-term goal is to minimize dependence on PX4 for control and estimation, we keep it in the stack to manage low-level flight infrastructure and safety-critical components.

docs.title: MAVLink
docs.text:
MAVLink is a lightweight communication protocol used to exchange messages between:

  • PX4 (flight controller)
  • Companion computers
  • Ground control stations (e.g. QGroundControl)

It defines standardized messages for telemetry, odometry, vehicle state, commands, parameters, and system status. MAVSDK abstracts this protocol and exposes a clean, robust API.

docs.title: MAVSDK in Our Architecture
docs.text:
In our architecture, MAVSDK acts as the bridge between PX4 and our ROS 2-based codebase.

A dedicated MAVSDK client is embedded inside ROS 2, allowing our autonomy, estimation, and control modules to communicate with the flight controller through a unified interface. MAVSDK handles all low-level communication, while our code focuses on high-level logic.

docs.title: Connecting to the Drone
docs.text:
The connection mechanism depends on the execution context:

  • PX4 SITL MAVSDK typically connects over UDP to a simulated PX4 instance (e.g. Gazebo).

  • Real hardware MAVSDK connects over serial (USB/UART) or UDP, depending on the companion computer and flight controller setup.

Once connected, MAVSDK manages system discovery, heartbeats, and link monitoring.

docs.title: Data Flow: PX4 → MAVSDK → ROS 2
docs.text:
Using the MAVSDK API, we retrieve:

  • Estimator outputs and telemetry
  • PX4 odometry (position, velocity, orientation)
  • Vehicle status
  • Arming state
  • Flight mode
  • System health and failsafe status

This data is forwarded to ROS 2 and consumed by higher-level modules.

docs.title: Standard PX4 Control Path
docs.text:
By default, MAVSDK offboard commands rely on PX4’s cascaded PID control architecture. Commands such as body rates and collective thrust are processed by PX4 controllers before being converted into actuator outputs.

This mode is useful for safety and rapid prototyping, but it constrains full control authority.

docs.title: Direct Per-Motor Thrust Control
docs.text:
Our primary objective is to bypass PX4’s internal control loops and directly command the actuators. We therefore support per-motor thrust commands, enabling:

  • Full control authority for MPC or RL policies
  • Independence from PX4’s cascaded PID controllers
  • Clear separation between control logic and hardware interfacing

In this setup, MAVSDK is used purely as a helper for low-level communication and system management, not as a control algorithm.

docs.title: Why We Keep MAVSDK and PX4
docs.text:
Even when bypassing PX4 controllers and estimation, we retain both components because they provide:

  • Robust communication and system management (via MAVSDK)
  • Access to telemetry, status, and safety mechanisms
  • A reliable plan B using PX4’s native estimator and controllers if needed

In the long term, PX4 and MAVSDK may no longer be required, but for now we keep them to manage the interface layer handling low-level interaction with the vehicle.

In summary, MAVSDK is the communication backbone between PX4 and our ROS 2 autonomy stack, while PX4 serves as a modular, tool-rich, and safety-capable platform that we can fall back on when necessary.

docs.title: Model Predictive Control (MPC)
docs.text:
Page Owner: Mattia De Martino, Michalis Papadakis

This section documents the Model Predictive Control (MPC) implementation contained in the mpc folder. The MPC is implemented using CasADi for symbolic modeling and ACADOS for solving the nonlinear optimal control problem (OCP).

The controller computes total thrust and body-rate commands, which are later converted into MAVSDK offboard commands.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The MPC implementation is structured into three main components:

  1. drone_model.py – Drone dynamics and constraints
  2. drone_opt.py – ACADOS optimal control problem and solver
  3. drone_mpc_controller.py – High-level MPC controller interface

The execution flow is:

  • Current state and reference are provided to the MPC controller
  • The optimizer solves a finite-horizon OCP
  • The first control input is extracted
  • The command is converted to a MAVSDK-compatible AttitudeRate

docs.title: Drone Dynamics Model (drone_model.py)
docs.text: This file defines the drone model used by the MPC and exports it in a format compatible with ACADOS.

docs.title: State Definition
docs.text:
The state vector has 13 dimensions:

  • Position p (3): NED frame
  • Velocity v (3): NED frame
  • Quaternion q (4): body → NED
  • Body angular rates w (3)

docs.title: Control Inputs
docs.text:
The control vector has 4 inputs:

  • Total thrust (N)
  • Body rate commands: roll, pitch, yaw (rad/s)

docs.title: Dynamics
docs.text:
The model includes:

  • Position dynamics Position derivative equals velocity.

  • Translational dynamics Thrust is applied in the body frame and rotated to the NED frame using the quaternion. Gravity is applied in the NED frame. An optional drag term is present but set to zero.

  • Quaternion kinematics Quaternion derivative is computed from body angular rates. The quaternion is normalized to avoid numerical drift.

  • Angular rate dynamics Angular rates follow a first-order tracking model: w_dot = (w_cmd - w) / tau_w

docs.title: Physical Parameters and Constraints
docs.text:
The model includes: - Mass and inertia - Maximum thrust derived from motor parameters - Thrust limits - Body rate limits - Bounds on: - Angular rates - Velocity - Position

All constraints are stored and later used by the optimizer.

docs.title: ACADOS Model Export
docs.text:
The model is exported with: - Explicit and implicit dynamics - State and control definitions - Constraint information

This allows direct integration into an ACADOS OCP.

docs.title: MPC Optimizer (drone_opt.py)
docs.text:
This file defines and solves the nonlinear OCP using ACADOS.

[!NOTE] API Compatibility: The implementation in drone_opt.py is compatible with both legacy and newer versions of acados_template. It automatically detects if paths should be set via environment variables or manual properties.

docs.title: Horizon Setup
docs.text:
• Prediction horizon: T
  • Number of nodes: N

docs.title: Cost Function
docs.text: An external nonlinear cost is used.

docs.title: Stage Cost
docs.text: The stage cost penalizes: - Position error - Velocity error - Quaternion error (Euclidean difference) - Angular rate error - Control effort (thrust deviation from hover and body rates)

docs.title: Terminal Cost
docs.text: The terminal cost penalizes: - Position error - Velocity error - Quaternion error - Angular rate error

docs.title: Parameters and References
docs.text: The reference state is passed as a parameter to the solver. The optimizer supports: - Point-to-point control - Reference trajectory tracking

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: The optimizer enforces: - Control bounds (thrust and body rates) - State bounds on angular rates - Fixed initial state at the beginning of each solve

docs.title: MPC Solve Step
docs.text:
At each control step: 1. The current state is normalized (quaternion) 2. References are set for all nodes 3. The solver is initialized (with warm start if available) 4. The OCP is solved 5. The first control input is extracted

If the solver fails, an exception is raised and logged.

docs.title: MPC Controller Interface (drone_mpc_controller.py)
docs.text: This file provides the interface between the MPC and the rest of the system.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text: The controller: - Initializes the drone model and optimizer - Receives the current state estimate - Receives a goal position or reference trajectory - Calls the optimizer

docs.title: Control Output
docs.text:
The MPC outputs: - Thrust in Newtons - Body rates in rad/s

These are converted to: - Normalized thrust in [0, 1] - Body rates in degrees per second

The final output is a MAVSDK AttitudeRate command.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: If the optimizer fails: - A safe hover command is returned - Debug information can be logged for analysis

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The MPC module provides: - A physically consistent drone model - A constrained nonlinear MPC formulation - A clear interface for integration with the flight stack

It is currently the main controller implemented in the codebase and serves as the reference control implementation.

docs.title: Betaflight MSP Control Architecture
docs.text: This section describes how the ETHRC Drone Racing framework bridges autonomous high-level control commands (such as those from an MPC or RL agent) directly into the Betaflight flight controller.

docs.title: Introduction to Hardware-in-the-Loop Control
docs.text:
For autonomous flight, the companion computer (NVIDIA Jetson) must be able to inject flight commands into the drone's flight controller, substituting the pilot's traditional remote control sticks.

While many robotics autopilots (like PX4 or ArduPilot) utilize MAVLink for receiving these commands, Betaflight operates natively on the Multiwii Serial Protocol (MSP). Therefore, the most native, low-latency, and reliable method to control a Betaflight drone via a companion computer is to stream MSP packets directly over a serial connection.

This architecture allows an external computer to "override" the pilot's stick inputs seamlessly while keeping the pilot in the loop with a physical safety switch.

docs.title: Software Architecture
docs.text:
The control pipeline from the autonomous planner down to the flight controller consists of two ROS 2 nodes connected in sequence:

  1. betaflight_msp_controller (The Translation Bridge)
  2. multiwii2_node (The Serial Driver)

docs.title: 1. betaflight_msp_controller (Translation Bridge)
docs.text:
The high-level controllers (e.g., drone_controller_node) output standardized robotics commands—specifically thrust values and rotational rates (roll, pitch, yaw in degrees per second)—to the /drone_attitude_cmd topic.

Betaflight, however, expects these values as Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) signals ranging from 1000 to 2000 on specific channels (Aileron, Elevator, Rudder, Throttle). The betaflight_msp_controller node subscribes to the continuous stream of attitude commands and mathematically maps them into 1000-2000 PWM signals.

Configurable Parameters: * attitude_cmd_topic (string): The input topic name to listen to. Default: '/drone_attitude_cmd' * rc_override_topic (string): The output topic where the OverrideRCIn message will be published. Default: '/multiwii/rc/override' * max_rate_deg_s (float): The maximum rotational rate (in degrees per second) that corresponds to maximum stick deflection (a PWM of 2000 or 1000). Default: 500.0. * Example: If max_rate_deg_s is 500, an incoming roll rate command of 250.0 translates mathematically to a center-offset PWM of 1750.

docs.title: 2. multiwii2_node (Serial Driver)
docs.text: Once the commands are accurately mapped to the 1000-2000 range, they are sent as mavros_msgs/msg/OverrideRCIn messages to the multiwii_ros2 node. This open-source C++ node is responsible for managing the actual serial hardware (/dev/ttyACM0 via USB/UART). It converts the structured ROS message into an MSP_SET_RAW_RC binary packet and transmits it over the serial lines to the flight controller.

docs.title: Betaflight FC Configuration
docs.text: To enable this architecture, the flight controller must be running Betaflight version 4.5.2 or higher (4.6 is officially recommended by high-performance MSP libraries like Deonixlive) and configured to trust the Jetson's manual serial inputs.

docs.title: 1. Enable MSP on the Port
docs.text: Connect the Jetson to the Flight Controller (typically via an available UART or the USB-C connection exposing /dev/ttyACM0). In the Betaflight Configurator > Ports tab, ensure that the Configuration/MSP toggle is enabled for the port physically connected to the Jetson. If you're using high update frequencies, use a high Baud rate (e.g., 1000000 or 115200).

docs.title: 2. Configure the MSP Channels Mask in CLI
docs.text:
Betaflight strictly limits which radio channels an external computer can override for safety. You must manually unlock the Roll, Pitch, Yaw, and Throttle channels by defining the msp_override_channels_mask.

The bits in the mask correlate to: AUX16 | ... | AUX2 | AUX1 | YAW | THROTTLE | PITCH | ROLL. Setting a bit to 1 enables the override.

  • Warning: It is highly advised against overwriting AUX1 because the ARMING switch is typically located there. Let the human pilot retain arming authority!

Open the CLI tab in Betaflight Configurator and paste one of the following commands based on your needs:

docs.title: Common Override Examples
docs.text:
1. Standard Autonomous Flight (Roll, Pitch, Yaw, Throttle) This is the most common setup. It grants the Jetson full directional control. 

set msp_override_channels_mask = 15
save

2. Throttle Test Mode (Throttle Only) Useful when initially tuning the PID hover values. The Jetson only controls altitude (Throttle = Bit 3 = 4), while you maintain standard Roll, Pitch, and Yaw via your remote. 

set msp_override_channels_mask = 4
save

3. Flight + Payload Drop (AETR + AUX2) If the Jetson also needs to trigger a servo or payload drop mechanism located on AUX2 (Bit 6 = 32). 32 + 15 = 47. 

set msp_override_channels_mask = 47
save

(Tip: If you notice during testing that the Yaw and Throttle seem reversed, verify that Betaflight hasn't swapped the internal YAW/THROTTLE channel order inside your specific version's MSP parser).

docs.title: 3. Configure MSP Override (Safety Switch)
docs.text:
To ensure the pilot maintains ultimate authority over the drone, we utilize Betaflight's built-in MSP Override mode.

  1. Navigate to the Modes tab in the Betaflight Configurator.
  2. Locate the MSP OVERRIDE mode.
  3. Assign this mode to a physical switch on your RC Transmitter (e.g., AUX2 or AUX3).

How it works during a flight: * Switch OFF (Manual Mode): Betaflight strictly listens to your radio receiver. The Jetson is continuously generating and sending autonomous flight commands into the void; Betaflight safely ignores them. * Switch ON (Autonomous Mode): Betaflight seamlessly transfers control of the Roll, Pitch, Yaw, and Throttle channels (due to our mask of 15) over to the continuous stream of MSP_SET_RAW_RC packets provided by the Jetson. * If the drone begins to act erratically, the human pilot immediately flips the switch back to OFF, instantly regaining manual control.

docs.title: Advanced: MSP Extensions (Controlling More)
docs.text:
While MSP_SET_RAW_RC is sufficient for standard flight stick emulation, Betaflight also supports a suite of broader MSP Extensions.

Should we ever need to "control more" than just the flight axes, these extensions allow the Jetson to dig deeper into the actual state machine and configuration of the flight controller in real-time. For example:

  • MSP_SET_MODE_RANGE: Instead of relying on the human pilot to pre-configure physical AUX switches to trigger functions like Angle Mode, Acro Trainer, or Beeper, the Jetson can programmatically redefine mode ranges on the fly.
  • MSP_SET_ADJUSTMENT_RANGE: If the high-level Reinforcement Learning (RL) or MPC node determines that the drone's PID tuning is no longer optimal due to battery sag or turbulence, it can use MSP adjustment ranges to dynamically push changes to the PID loops mid-flight.
  • Other Integrations: Broader MSP commands also allow the companion computer to push custom text directly to the pilot's OSD (On-Screen Display), change Video Transmitter (VTX) power levels, or change LED Strip configurations based on the Jetson's perception state.

To utilize these advanced extensions in the future, the multiwii2_node or a direct serial driver would need to be expanded to accept and serialize these specific Betaflight API commands.

docs.title: Running the Pipeline
docs.text: There are two primary ways to run the control pipeline: via individual nodes or using the unified "Racing Bringup" script.

docs.title: 1. Unified Racing Bringup (Recommended)
docs.text:
This script starts the entire stack (Comms, Perception, and Control) in one go. It is the fastest way to get to a flight-ready state.

ros2 launch drone_control racing_bringup.launch.py msp_port:=/dev/ttyTHS1

docs.title: 2. Manual Node Launch
docs.text:
If you need more granular control or are debugging a specific component, you can launch the MSP bridge individually:

# Launch with default YAML parameters (ttyTHS1, 1.5Mbps)
ros2 launch betaflight_msp_controller msp_bridge.launch.py

# Launch with CLI overrides
ros2 launch betaflight_msp_controller msp_bridge.launch.py port:=/dev/ttyUSB0 baudrate:=115200

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The system supports two levels of configuration:

  1. YAML Parameters: Defaults are stored in src/betaflight_msp_controller/config/msp_params.yaml. Edit this file to set your "permanent" hardware setup.
  2. CLI Arguments: Any parameter in the YAML can be overridden at runtime using the name:=value syntax in the launch command.

docs.title: Testing Without a Radio Controller
docs.text: In development environments where a physical RC Transmitter is unavailable, you can use the arm_and_override_persistent.py utility script to simulate the radio link and inject autonomous commands simultaneously.

docs.title: Persistent Arm & Override Logic
docs.text: This script utilizes two separate serial connections to the Flight Controller: 1. Primary RX (USB): Emulates the RC Receiver, sending continuous heartbeat packets for ARMing (AUX1) and enabling MSP_OVERRIDE mode (AUX2). 2. Override Port (UART): Sends the actual AETR stick values (Roll, Pitch, Yaw, Throttle) that will bypass the primary RX while the override switch is active.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Run the script from the Jetson (ensure permissions are set for /dev/ttyACM* and /dev/ttyTHS*): 

python3 scripts/msp/arm_and_override_persistent.py /dev/ttyACM0 /dev/ttyTHS1

Safety Features: * Initialization: Sends 1 second of zero throttle/disarmed packets to clear Betaflight's boot safety checks. * Heartbeat: Maintains a 50Hz (20ms) update rate to prevent failsafes. * Emergency Stop: Pressing Ctrl+C immediately sends a burst of Disarm packets and zeroes all channels before closing the ports.

docs.title: 1. Serial Port Permissions
docs.text:
If the node fails to open the serial port with a "Permission Denied" error, your user likely lacks the necessary group permissions. Solution: Add your user to the dialout and tty groups, then log out and back in. 

sudo usermod -a -G dialout,tty $USER

docs.title: 2. Package Discovery (Colcon)
docs.text: The betaflight_msp_controller was moved to the top-level src/ directory to ensure colcon finds it. If you move it back inside another package, ros2 launch will fail to find it.

docs.title: 3. Baud Rate Mismatch
docs.text: Betaflight's msp_baudrate (visible in the Ports tab) must match the Jetson's baud rate. If they differ, the node will "connect" but no data will be parsed by the FC. * Default Project Baud: 1500000 (1.5 Mbps) for high-rate IMU streaming.

docs.title: 4. Cable Quality
docs.text: Always use a high-quality data cable. Many USB cables included with consumer electronics are "charging only" and do not have the data lines connected, which will result in the device not appearing in /dev/.

docs.title: 5. Proper Orientation
docs.text: If the drone pitches when you command roll, check your Betaflight Board Alignment settings and ensure the max_rate_deg_s in msp_params.yaml matches your high-level controller's expectations.

docs.title: Testing Without Props
docs.text: IMPORTANT: Always test your MSP override configuration WITHOUT PROPELLERS. 1. Launch the msp_bridge.launch.py. 2. Connect the FC to Betaflight Configurator. 3. Use the Receiver Tab to verify that sending commands from ROS 2 actually moves the Roll/Pitch/Yaw/Throttle sliders in real-time.

docs.text: Page Owner: Ishaan Jain, Mahmoud El Minawi, Maté Tirpak

docs.title: 3. Start IsaacLab (Docker-Based Setup)

docs.title: 7. Overview of the Current Environment Setup
docs.text: The provided QuadcopterEnvCopy environment is a modified version of the default IsaacLab quadcopter task. It introduces a time-based circular trajectory that the drone must follow, along with small vertical oscillations.

docs.title: What the Drone Is Trained to Do
docs.text:
The quadrotor is trained using reinforcement learning to:

  • Track a moving goal position that follows a circular path around each environment's origin.
  • Maintain stable flight while adjusting thrust and rotational moments.
  • Minimize:
  • linear velocity error
  • angular velocity error
  • distance to the moving goal

docs.title: How the Trajectory Works
docs.text:
Each environment receives: - A unique random phase offset (so not all drones fly in sync), - A circular XY path with adjustable radius and period, - A small vertical oscillation added to the Z position.

The desired trajectory is computed every step and used to generate: - Observations (target position in the quadrotor’s body frame), - Rewards (distance-to-goal mapping, velocity penalties), - Done conditions (crashing or flying too high).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: In its current form, the drone learns to fly smoothly along a dynamic circular trajectory, staying close to a moving 3D point while maintaining stable and efficient control. This setup is ideal for testing trajectory tracking, stability control, and low-level motor policy behavior.

docs.title: IMX219 90Hz High-Speed Tuning
docs.text:
This guide provides a procedure to enable 90Hz/92Hz capture with a Full 155° FOV on the Jetson Orin NX.

[!NOTE] Hardware Context: While this solution was developed and verified using the Seeed Studio A603 carrier board, the core sensor and timing modifications are applicable to any standard Jetson Orin NX setup. Users with different carrier boards should primarily verify the Device Tree pinmux and clock assignments.

[!IMPORTANT] Environment Tested: This solution has been verified on Ubuntu 22.04 LTS running JetPack 6.2 (L4T R36.4.3). It assumes you are working within the standard NVIDIA Linux for Tegra (L4T) source tree on a host PC or directly on the Jetson.

docs.title: 📋 Prerequisites & Filesystem
docs.text: We assume a standard L4T directory structure. Let $L4T_DIR be your base directory (e.g., ~/nvidia/nvidia_sdk/JetPack_6.2_Linux_JETSON_ORIN_NX_TARGETS/Linux_for_Tegra/).

docs.title: 1. Extracting Sources
docs.text:
If you haven't already, extract the Out-of-Tree (OOT) driver sources provided by NVIDIA: 

cd $L4T_DIR/source
tar -xjf kernel_oot_modules_src.tbz2
# This creates the 'nvidia-oot' directory

docs.title: 2. Tools
docs.text: • Ensure dtc (Device Tree Compiler) is installed: sudo apt install device-tree-compiler.

docs.title: 🛠 Step 2: Sensor Driver Patches
docs.text:
You must modify the registration tables in the nvidia-oot driver to align the physical sensor timing with 90Hz logic.

  • File Path: source/nvidia-oot/drivers/media/i2c/imx219_mode_tbls.h

docs.title: 2.1 Timing & Exposure Guard
docs.text: Modify the imx219_mode_1280x720_60fps table (which we repurpose for 90Hz): - Exposure (592 lines): Set {0x015A, 0x02} and {0x015B, 0x50}. - VMAX (633 lines): Set {0x0160, 0x02} and {0x0161, 0x79}. - Line Length (4000 lines): Set {0x0162, 0x0F} and {0x0163, 0xA0}.

docs.title: 2.2 Full-FOV Reduction (4x4)
docs.text: To map the full 155° sensor area instead of a crop, combine Analog Binning with Subsampling: - X/Y_ODD_INC (2x2 Skip): {0x0170, 0x03}, {0x0171, 0x03}. - BINNING_MODE (2x2 Analog Bin): {0x0174, 0x03}, {0x0175, 0x03}.

docs.title: 2.3 CSI Protocol Stability
docs.text: • Data Format (RAW10): Ensure {0x018C, 0x0A} and {0x018D, 0x0A}.

docs.title: 🏗 Step 3: Device Tree Turbo-Drain
docs.text:
The Jetson's Video Input (VI) pipeline must drain the CSI FIFO faster than the sensor's output to prevent overflows at high framerates.

  1. Locate the imx219@10 node in your carrier board's DTS (e.g., tegra234-p3768-0000-a0.dts).
  2. Update the pix_clk_hz property: 
    // Force 400MHz host drainage priority
pix_clk_hz = "400000000";

docs.title: 🚀 Step 4: Build & Deploy
docs.text:
1. Compile: Navigate to the nvidia-oot root and run make modules.
  2. Install: 
    # Copy the compiled module to the target updates directory
sudo cp nv_imx219.ko /usr/lib/modules/$(uname -r)/updates/drivers/media/i2c/
sudo depmod -a
  3. Reboot: A full power cycle is recommended to clear the sensor logic and apply the new Device Tree configuration.

docs.title: ⚠️ Known Pitfalls & Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Probable Cause Fix Black Screen Exposure > Frame Length Ensure Exposure = 592 and VMAX = 633. CSI Timeout Protocol Mismatch Verify 0x018C/D is 0x0A (RAW10). Quarter FOV Binning Only Ensure BOTH Binning AND Skipping bits are set to 0x03. FIFO Overflow Low Host Clock Verify pix_clk_hz is strictly 400000000.

docs.title: VIO & IMU Synchronization (Sub-Microsecond)
docs.text: To achieve stable state estimation (VIO) at the speeds required for autonomous drone racing (>20 m/s), high-precision synchronization between the IMU and the camera frame start is non-negotiable. This document details the "Hard-Sync" architecture using the Jetson Hardware Timestamping Engine (HTE).

docs.title: 🏗 The Hard-Sync Architecture
docs.text: Instead of relying on soft-timestamps (Argus arrival time), we use a dedicated electrical pulse to correlate the Flight Controller (FC) and Jetson clocks.

docs.title: 1. External Trigger (Kakute H7)
docs.text: We repurpose the M6 (MAIN6) motor pin on the Kakute H7 v1.5 as a camera trigger. - Signal: 3.3V Pulse (High for 1ms) per frame integration start. - Firmware (PX4): - Set TRIG_INTERFACE to 1 (GPIO). - Set TRIG_PINS to 6 (remapping M6). - Set TRIG_MODE to 1 (triggered on integration).

docs.title: 2. Hardware Timestamping (Jetson Orin NX)
docs.text: The pulse from M6 is connected to an Always On (AON) GPIO on the Jetson Orin NX header. - Target Pin: Pin 31 (SoC: GPIO3_PAA.00). - Feature: Hardware Timestamping Engine (HTE) in JetPack 6.2. - Clock: The HTE timestamps the rising edge in the TSC (Time Stamp Counter) domain, providing sub-microsecond accuracy independent of CPU load or interrupt latency.

docs.title: 🛠 Hardware Wiring
docs.text:
Connection Kakute H7 (FC) Seeed A603 (Jetson) Notes Sync Signal M6 (Signal Pin) Header Pin 31 3.3V Logic Level Ground ESC Ground Header Pin 39 Common reference is critical

[!WARNING] Ensure the Flight Controller and Jetson share a common ground. If powered by separate regulators, verify there is no ground loop.

docs.title: 🏁 High-Rate Betaflight Integration (Betaflight)
docs.text: For ultra-low latency configurations, we support a 2000Hz IMU stream using the Betaflight Serial Blackbox methodology.

docs.title: 1. External Trigger (Betaflight)
docs.text:
We repurpose a PinIO-capable pad (e.g., LED_STRIP) to generate a sync pulse. - Signal: 3.3V Pulse (High for 1ms) triggered by USER1 mode. - Betaflight CLI: 

resource LED_STRIP 1 NONE
resource PINIO 1 <PAD_RESOURCE>
set pinio_config = 1,1,1,1
set pinio_box = 40,255,255,255
save

docs.title: 2. Hardware Timestamping (Pin 16)
docs.text: The Betaflight sync pulse is connected to Pin 16 (SoC: GPIO3_PBB.01) on the Jetson Orin NX. - HTE: This pin is part of the AON domain and supports raw hardware timestamping via the HTE peripheral.

docs.title: 1. Device Tree Patch (JETSON-SIDE)
docs.text:
To enable HTE on Pin 31, you must patch the device tree to include the HTE test driver or a custom VIO-Sync driver:

// Fragment for tegra-hte-test
tegra_hte_test {
    status = "okay";
    gpio-controller = <&tegra_aon_gpio>;
    // Map to PAA.00 (Pin 31)
    hte-gpios = <&tegra_aon_gpio TEGRA234_AON_GPIO(AA, 0) GPIO_ACTIVE_HIGH>;
};

docs.title: 2. Clock Correlation Logic
docs.text:
The VIO node (OpenVINS / Rovioli) should consume: 1. IMU Samples: Received via Micro-XRCE-DDS with FC timestamps. 2. HTE Pulses: Extracted from /dev/hte_test (or kernel events). 3. Camera Frames: Received via Argus.

Synchronization math: $$T_{offset} = T_{HTE_Timestamp} - T_{FC_Trigger_Msg}$$ This offset is tracked using a Kalman Filter to account for clock drift between the STM32H7 (FC) and the Orin NX.

docs.title: ⏰ System Time Synchronization (Jetson Orin NX)
docs.text: Before performing any hardware-triggered synchronization, ensure the Jetson system clock is aligned with the ground station/capture host. This is critical for TLS/Docker stability and long-term clock drift compensation.

docs.title: Tool: sync_time.sh
docs.text:
Use the provided utility to synchronize the boreas clock with your local ground station: 

./scripts/tools/remote/sync_time.sh
This script captures the current UTC time from the GS and applies it to the remote Jetson via SSH, bypassing issues with volatile RTCs on developer hardware.

  • NVIDIA HTE Guide: Documentation for Hardware Timestamping in JP6.
  • PX4 User Guide: Camera Trigger Configuration.

docs.title: Using ECR Images with Docker Compose
docs.text: If you want to use a pre-built image from ECR with docker compose (e.g., to skip the slow local build of the dev target), you can use the Tag Trick.

docs.title: The "Tag Trick"
docs.text:
Docker Compose identifies images locally by the project name and service name (e.g., ethrc-drone-racing-dev). To force Compose to use an ECR image:

  1. Pull the ECR image: 
    make pull REPO=aeronautics/droneracing/main/dev TAG=latest
  2. Tag it locally to match the Compose name: 
    docker tag 916780037007.dkr.ecr.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/aeronautics/droneracing/main/dev:latest ethrc-drone-racing-dev:latest
  3. Start Compose as usual: 
    docker compose up -d dev
    Now, docker compose exec -it dev bash will put you inside a container running the official CI build.

docs.title: CI Workflow
docs.text:
The aws_ecr.yml GitHub Actions workflow handles automated builds. It:

  1. Detects which targets have changed by diffing against the last successful run's commit SHA
  2. If no prior successful run exists (new branch), all targets are built
  3. Builds only affected targets in parallel
  4. Pushes each image with a short SHA tag and latest
  5. Uses Docker BuildKit registry cache stored in ECR to accelerate incremental builds

docs.text:

gh workflow run aws_ecr.yml --ref <your-branch> -f force_all=true

docs.title: Perception Stack Overview
docs.text: The perception stack is responsible for providing a reliable, drift-free state estimate of the drone in the world frame. It achieves this by fusing high-frequency relative odometry with sparse absolute pose corrections.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
The system follows a tiered architecture for pose estimation:

graph TD
    subgraph Sensors
        Cam["Camera (Mono/Stereo)"]
        IMU["IMU (Accel/Gyro)"]
        Vicon["Vicon (Optional)"]
    end

    subgraph "Local Odometry"
        VIO["OpenVINS (VIO)"]
    end

    subgraph "Absolute Corrections"
        Gate["Gate Detection (WIP)"]
    end

    subgraph "Fusion Layer"
        EKF["EKF (robot_localization)"]
    end

    Cam --> VIO
    IMU --> VIO
    VIO -->|"/ov_msckf/odomimu (Odom)"| EKF

    Cam --> Gate
    Gate -->|"/gate_detection/drone_pose (Pose)"| EKF


    Vicon -->|"(Indoor GT)"| EKF

    EKF -->|"/odometry/filtered"| Control["Control & Planning"]

docs.title: Topic Mappings
docs.text:
The following table summarizes the data flow between perception modules.

Source Module Topic Name Message Type Frequency Consumer Sensors /cam0/image_raw sensor_msgs/Image 30 Hz VIO, Gate Detection Sensors /imu0 sensor_msgs/Imu 200 Hz VIO OpenVINS /ov_msckf/odomimu nav_msgs/Odometry 100 Hz EKF Gate Detection /gate_detection/drone_pose PoseWithCovarianceStamped 10-30 Hz EKF Vicon /vicon/drone/drone geometry_msgs/Transform 100 Hz EKF EKF /odometry/filtered nav_msgs/Odometry 100 Hz Control

docs.title: Coordinate Systems
docs.text:
The perception stack utilizes the standard ROS 2 (REP-103) coordinate conventions:

  • world Frame: Global fixed frame. Its origin is typically defined at the start of the mission.
  • odom Frame: A locally stable frame provided by the EKF. It is continuous (no jumps) but may drift relative to the world frame over long durations if absolute fixes are lost.
  • base_link Frame: The center of mass of the drone.
    • X-axis: Forward
    • Y-axis: Left
    • Z-axis: Up

docs.title: 1. Visual-Inertial Odometry (OpenVINS)
docs.text: The VIO component uses the open_vins library to fuse camera images and IMU data. - Formulation: Implements an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) with a Multi-State Constraint Kalman Filter (MSCKF). - Constraint-Based: It avoids estimating feature positions in the main filter state, making it highly efficient for high-speed flight. - Online Calibration: Online-calibrates the rotation and translation between the Camera and IMU. - Output: Published as nav_msgs/Odometry on /ov_msckf/odomimu.

docs.title: 2. Gate Detection & PnP (WIP)
docs.text: The Gate Detection component identifies racing gates and estimates the drone's pose relative to them. - Deep Learning: Uses a U-Net based segmentation network (GateNet) to detect gate masks. - QuAdGate: Extracts sub-pixel corner candidates and matches them using geometric descriptors. - PnP Solver: Uses cv2.solvePnP to find the absolute translation and rotation from the known gate dimensions to the observed pixel coordinates. - Output: Published as geometry_msgs/PoseWithCovarianceStamped on /gate_detection/drone_pose.

docs.title: 3. Fusion Logic (The EKF)
docs.text: The system uses robot_localization with Smooth Lagged Data support. - Rewind/Fast-Forward: Vision processing takes time (50-100ms). The EKF maintains a history of past states, "rewinds" to the image timestamp to fuse the delayed measurement, and then re-propagates the state to the current time. - Output: The definitive state estimate on /odometry/filtered.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text: For deeper technical details on individual components, see: - VIO (OpenVINS) - Gate Detection - Sensor Fusion (EKF) - Vicon Tracking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: We provide an ArUco marker [DICT_5x5_1000] detection system serving as an initial gate detection pipeline and as a fallback ground truth method. The markers have to be physically placed in the environment, subsequently ground truth location and the size of the markers have to be parsed into the system.

docs.title: Input Topics
docs.text: The ArUco pose estimation system subscribes to the following ROS2 topics:

docs.title: Camera Images
docs.text:
• /cam0/image_raw

  • Type: sensor_msgs/msg/Image

  • Description: Raw camera images from a single camera
  • Frequency: Typically 20-30 Hz

docs.title: Output Topics
docs.text: The ArUco pose estimations system publishes the following ROS 2 topics (under namespace /aruco by default):

docs.title: Diagnostic
docs.text:
• /aruco/camera_pose

    • Type: geometry_msgs::msg::PoseStamped
    • Description: Publishes the pose and location of the camera

  • /aruco/drone_pose

    • Type: geometry_msgs::msg::PoseWithCovarianceStamped
    • Description: Publishes the pose and location of the drone

  • /aruco/visualization_markers

    • Type: visualization_msgs::msg::Marker
    • Description: Publishes point cloud markers (for e.g. rviz2) to show the pose and location of the drone

  • /aruco/diagnostics

    • Type: diagnostic_msgs::msg::DiagnosticArray
    • Description: Publishes the values in the terminal

docs.title: Brief explanation
docs.text:
This section provides a short walkthrough and explanation of the detection system:

  1. Configuration: as mentioned in the overview, parse the marker ID, pose, and size into a YAML file in config/.

  2. Detection: we utilize the marker detection library from OpenCV and enhance the performance with Lucas-Kanade optical flow and a smoothening factor.

  3. Visual Update: the borders of the detected markers will be highlighted.

  4. Output: The estimated pose is published as a 6-DoF transform consisting of:

  5. Position: (x, y, z)
  6. Orientation: quaternion (x, y, z, w)

docs.title: Launch ArUco Marker Estimation in Gazebo Simulation
docs.text: ros2 launch aruco_pose_estimation aruco_pose_estimation.launch.py

docs.title: Extended Kalman Filter (EKF)
docs.text: Page Owner: Oliver Calvet

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The EKF package provides sensor fusion for drone state estimation by leveraging the Robot Localization package's Extended Kalman Filter implementation. The filter fuses visual-inertial odometry (VIO) from OpenVINS with absolute pose measurements from ArUco marker detection to produce a robust, high-frequency state estimate. The current implementation uses the standard robot_localization package without drone-specific model adaptations.

docs.title: Input Topics
docs.text: The EKF system subscribes to the following ROS 2 topics. Orientation data arrives as quaternions but is internally converted to roll, pitch, yaw (RPY) for the filter's 15-dimensional state vector: [x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw, vx, vy, vz, vroll, vpitch, vyaw, ax, ay, az].

docs.title: VIO Odometry
docs.text:
• Topic: /ov_msckf/odomimu
  • Type: nav_msgs/msg/Odometry
  • Description: Odometry from OpenVINS containing pose (position + orientation) and velocity estimates
  • Used for Update: x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw, vx, vy, vz, vroll, vpitch, vyaw

docs.title: ArUco Pose
docs.text:
• Topic: /aruco/drone_pose
  • Type: geometry_msgs/msg/PoseWithCovarianceStamped
  • Description: Absolute pose measurements from ArUco marker detection
  • Used for Update: x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw

docs.title: Control Input (Optional)
docs.text:
• Topic: /control/command (remapped from cmd_vel)
  • Type: geometry_msgs/msg/Twist
  • Description: Velocity commands used for motion prediction (currently disabled)

docs.title: Output Topics
docs.text: The EKF system publishes the following ROS 2 topics:

docs.title: Fused Odometry
docs.text:
• /ekf/odometry
  • Type: nav_msgs/msg/Odometry
  • Description: Fused state estimate containing pose and velocity with covariances
  • Frequency: 100 Hz (configurable via frequency parameter)

docs.title: Acceleration
docs.text:
• /accel/filtered
  • Type: geometry_msgs/msg/AccelWithCovarianceStamped
  • Description: Estimated linear acceleration

docs.title: Transforms (TF)
docs.text:
• /tf
  • Description: Transform from world frame to base_link frame via odom frame
  • Frequency: 100 Hz

docs.title: Brief Explanation
docs.text:
The sensor fusion pipeline works as follows:

  1. Prediction Step: The filter propagates the state estimate forward in time using a constant-velocity motion model. The prediction runs at 100 Hz to maintain smooth state estimates.

  2. VIO Update: When odometry messages arrive from OpenVINS (/ov_msckf/odomimu), the filter incorporates full pose and velocity information (x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw, vx, vy, vz, vroll, vpitch, vyaw) to update the state estimate.

  3. Vision Update: Absolute pose measurements from ArUco marker detection (/aruco/drone_pose) provide global corrections to prevent drift. Only pose states (x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw) are fused from this source.

  4. Delayed Measurement Handling: The filter maintains a 0.5-second state history buffer (smooth_lagged_data: true) to properly handle out-of-order or delayed sensor measurements.

  5. Output: The fused state estimate is published as odometry and TF transforms for use by other modules.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The filter parameters are configured in config/rl_ekf.yaml. Key settings include:

Parameter Value Description frequency 100.0 Hz Filter update rate sensor_timeout 0.1 s Timeout before sensor is considered stale publish_tf true Publish TF transforms two_d_mode false Full 3D state estimation history_length 0.5 s State history for delayed measurements

docs.title: Frame Configuration
docs.text:
Frame Value Description map_frame world Global fixed reference frame for the environment odom_frame odom Continuous odometry frame (can drift over time) base_link_frame base_link Frame rigidly attached to the drone body world_frame world Reference frame for filter operation

Setting world_frame: world (same as map_frame) configures the filter to operate in the global map frame. This is required because we fuse absolute pose measurements from ArUco markers, which provide global corrections and eliminate drift. If world_frame were set to odom, the filter would only output continuous odometry without incorporating these global corrections.

docs.title: Launch EKF in Gazebo Simulation
docs.text:
ros2 launch ekf rl_ekf.launch.xml

This starts the robot_localization EKF node with fused odometry published on /ekf/odometry.

docs.title: Gate Detection & PnP Pose Estimation (WIP)
docs.text: Page Owner: Xander Yap

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Gate Detection module is a neural-network based vision system designed to provide absolute pose corrections for autonomous drone racing. It replaces the legacy ArUco-based system by detecting specialized racing gates and using the known geometry of the gates to calculate the drone's position and orientation via Perspective-n-Point (PnP).

[!IMPORTANT] This module is currently under active development (Work-in-Progress). The ROS 2 node and PnP solver are in a functional but experimental state.

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text:
The pipeline consists of three primary stages:

  1. Segmentation (GateNet): A U-Net style convolutional neural network that takes a raw camera image and produces a binary segmentation mask of the gate.
  2. Corner Extraction (QuAdGate): A geometric processing algorithm that:
    • Finds lines in the segmentation mask using LSD (Line Segment Detector).
    • Generates sub-pixel corner candidates from line intersections.
    • Matches candidates to known gate corner types (Outer TL/TR/BR/BL and Inner TL/TR/BR/BL) using shape descriptors.
  3. Pose Estimation (PnP): Uses cv2.solvePnP to map the 2D pixel coordinates of the detected corners to their 3D positions in the gate's local coordinate frame.

docs.title: detector_node
docs.text:
The primary real-time node that runs the full inference pipeline.

  • Subscribes to: /cam0/image_raw (sensor_msgs/Image)
  • Publishes to: /gate_detection/drone_pose (geometry_msgs/PoseWithCovarianceStamped)
  • Parameters:
    • checkpoint: Path to the .pth model file.
    • camera_topic: The image topic to subscribe to.
    • output_topic: The pose topic to publish.

docs.title: Launching
docs.text:
To launch the gate detection system within the perception stack:

ros2 launch gate_detection gate_detection.launch.py

docs.title: Development Tools
docs.text:
The package includes standalone scripts for dataset inspection and performance validation:

  • inference_standalone: Runs inference on a directory of images and generates a visual debug plot showing segmentation, line detection, and corner matching.
  • viewer_standalone: An interactive tool to review and clean synthetic datasets.

docs.title: Known Issues & TODOs
docs.text:
• [ ] Camera Intrinsics: Currently uses hardcoded placeholder values; needs to subscribe to camera_info.
  • [ ] Gate Dimensions: Dynamic loading of gate dimensions from a map configuration (similar to old ArUco YAMLs).
  • [ ] Temporal Filtering: Integration of a tracker to handle intermittent detections and motion blur.
  • [ ] Performance: Optimization for Jetson Orin NX (TensorRT conversion).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Vicon system provides accurate 6-DOF pose estimates (position and orientation) by tracking retroreflective markers attached to the drone using an array of infrared cameras. It is used as ground truth localization for indoor flights.

The ros2-vicon-receiver package connects to the Vicon DataStream SDK server running on the Vicon PC, retrieves tracking data at the camera frame rate, and publishes it as ROS 2 topics.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: We are using a VICON system with at least 5 MX-F40 cameras, which should be able to cover a cylinder with a diameter of 6m and roughly 5m height. To cover the full testing arena (8x8x5m), at least 7 cameras are recommended. This page describe the setup on a surface level, further details can be found in the Prophysics AG user manual

docs.title: Required Items
docs.text:
• Cameras: At least 5x MX-F40 cameras with mounting options (e.g., tripods).
  • Vicon Hub: Central connection unit.
  • Cables: Dedicated cables to connect cameras to the hub.
  • Host PC: Windows 11 PC with VICON Tracker 3 installed (Tracker 4 is not compatible).
  • Ethernet Cable: To connect the hub to the host PC.

[!CAUTION] Before connecting everything, power off the hub and ensure cameras are mounted securely. Due to component age, repairs are difficult, posing an operational risk. Take extreme caution!

docs.title: Installation Steps
docs.text:
1. Positioning: Place cameras in a circular pattern, pointing towards the center. Secure cables with strain relief.
  2. Routing: Route cables to the Vicon Hub cleanly, avoiding sharp bends or tension.
  3. Connection: Connect cables to the hub securely.
  4. Power On: Turn on the hub via the silver metallic button on the front.
  5. Software: Launch Tracker 3. Cameras should be recognized within a minute.
  6. Verification:
  7. LEDs on cameras should light up green.
  8. Select all cameras in Tracker 3 and open the Camera Preview tab to see live infrared view.
  9. If this fails, power off immediately and reach out to your lead.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Before utilising the VICON system, it must be calibrated to ensure accurate position estimation. The process is divided into three main phases in the Vicon Tracker 3 software.

docs.title: 1. Camera Masking
docs.text: Eliminate noise from static reflections or sunlight. - Go to the Calibrate tab. - Click Auto Mask to automatically ignore static points of light or reflections in the cameras' view. - Ensure the calibration volume is clear of moving reflective materials during this.

docs.title: 2. Camera Calibration (The Wand Wave)
docs.text: Calculate the physical coordinates, rotation, and lens properties of each camera. - In the Calibrate Cameras section, select your dynamic calibration object (Wand) from the dropdown. - Click Start to begin data capture. - Wave the Wand slowly throughout the entire intended capture volume, ensuring markers are visible to multiple cameras. Make sure to go into depth too. - The software will automatically complete this phase once sufficient coverage and tracking quality thresholds are met. If the errors are too high or if some cameras are missing, redo the calibration.

docs.title: 3. Setting the Volume Origin (The L-Frame)
docs.text:
Define the center (0,0,0) and rotational alignment (X, Y, Z axes) of the absolute coordinate frame. - Place the static calibration object (T-Frame) flat on the arena floor at the desired origin location. - In the Set Volume Origin section, select the corresponding T-Frame model. - Click Start to trace its static orientation. - Click Set Origin to lock the global zero point alignment.

[!IMPORTANT] A successful origin set will align the grid in the 3D Perspective view with your real-world lab floor layout coordinates.

docs.title: Output Topics
docs.text: For each tracked object (subject + segment pair defined in Vicon Tracker), the node automatically creates a publisher:

docs.title: Pose
docs.text:
• Topic: /vicon/<SubjectName>/<SegmentName>
  • Type: geometry_msgs/msg/PoseStamped
  • Description: 6-DOF pose of the tracked object expressed in the world (map) frame. Position is in meters; orientation is a quaternion. Header stamp is the estimated capture time.
  • Example: /vicon/drone/drone

docs.title: Latency
docs.text:
• Topic: /vicon/latency
  • Type: std_msgs/msg/Float64
  • Description: Total Vicon pipeline latency in seconds for each received frame (GetLatencyTotal()).

docs.title: Transforms (TF)
docs.text:
• /tf — Dynamic transform from the vicon frame to each <SubjectName>_<SegmentName> frame, broadcast every frame.
  • /tf_static — Static transform from map to vicon origin, set at launch via map_xyz and map_rpy parameters.

docs.title: Launch
docs.text:
ros2 launch vicon_receiver client.launch.py \
  hostname:=192.168.0.78 \
  topic_namespace:=vicon \
  buffer_size:=200 \
  world_frame:=map \
  vicon_frame:=vicon \
  map_xyz:='[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]' \
  map_rpy:='[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]' \
  map_rpy_in_degrees:=false

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Description hostname 127.0.0.1 IP address of the Vicon PC running the DataStream server buffer_size 200 DataStream SDK internal buffer size world_frame map Name of the world frame in TF vicon_frame vicon Name of the Vicon origin frame in TF map_xyz [0,0,0] Translation (meters) from world_frame to vicon origin map_rpy [0,0,0] Rotation (rad or deg) from world_frame to vicon origin map_rpy_in_degrees false Set to true if map_rpy values are in degrees

docs.title: Setting Up a Tracked Object
docs.text:
In Vicon Tracker software on the Vicon PC:

  1. Create a new object in Vicon Tracker, assign the markers, and give it a name (e.g. drone).
  2. The segment name defaults to the same as the subject name.
  3. The resulting ROS topic will be /vicon/drone/drone.

docs.title: Latency Compensation
docs.text: To achieve high-accuracy sensor fusion (e.g., in robot_localization EKF), the vicon_receiver node implements sub-millisecond latency compensation.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: The node calls GetLatencyTotal() from the Vicon DataStream SDK to retrieve the total transmission and processing delay of the current frame. This latency is subtracted from the node's current system time to calculate the exact capture time of the pose.

docs.title: Usage in EKF
docs.text:
The EKF node is configured with smooth_lagged_data: true to correctly process these delayed measurements. This ensures that the global pose estimatate remains consistent even during high-acceleration maneuvers where latency jitter would normally cause divergence.
